line: A vertical line with numbered stops; each stop says what happens and what the customer gets; the line fills as the reader passes.
Use a week strip only for dependent steps with a different result each. Otherwise print a compact list.
The steps as stops on a drawn route or transit line, stop names set like a line map.
The offer as a receipt: items, dotted leaders, a total, what is included ticked off under it.
Only with --carry figures: print the price first. A meter needs several different prices supported by the supplied rates.
Plans as rungs growing left to right, each saying only what it adds to the one before.
A list in two sizes like a board: categories in display type, items with leaders, one special set apart.
The product's central view built large, with three callouts pinned to real parts of it.
One frame; three to five use cases as click tabs that change what the frame shows.
The product in the middle, thin leader lines to labelled parts round it.
Two states under one draggable divider, or side by side: before and after, with and without.
A datasheet: a dimension drawing on one side, a ruled table with aligned units on the other.
One measured range as a horizontal scale with reference points the reader knows.
A command or code panel beside the result it produces; steps advance on click.
The layers of a product or service as stacked slabs, one line each, the top one lifted.
Figures in a ruled ledger with their sources as footnotes; one row set large.
Two or three bars comparing with and without; the difference is the label.
One figure from the brief set very large with its unit and one line of meaning.
Each project a wide row: picture one side, name and fact line the other, sides alternating.
A typographic index of every item (name, place, year); one picture changes with the row under the pointer or focus.
Many small frames in a grid like a photographer's sheet, three of them enlarged.
Rooms or goods as cards shaped like door signs or tags: number, size, price.
Goods standing on one drawn line, name and price under each; arrows move the shelf.
Print matching hours once. Use a day bar when the available hours differ.
A small drawn map: a few streets, water or a park, the place and two landmarks. No map tiles.
Address and hours set like the back of a postcard beside its picture side.
Two seasons or two times of day as a toggle over one picture area.
The people as a ruled list with roles and one line each; small equal portraits or initials.
The tools and materials of the trade laid out as a flat lay: real icons, swatches, samples.
A reading column with facts pulled large into the margin.
The history on a horizontal year axis; only dates the brief gives.
Questions as an index on the left that stays; the answers scroll on the right.
Terms with short definitions in three columns.
The game's world in one drawn frame whose light changes over four steps of a day.
Things of the game's world as a set of collectible cards with one stat line each.
Dated devlog posts as a notebook column, a picture with each.
Dates, guests and room in one row with a live total, docked under the hero.
Choices as chips (size, colour, set); the picture and the price follow.
Items with steppers and a running total, like an order pad.
Keep words on five wrap columns and take the photograph from the next column to the screen edge. Alternate sides on a repeat.
Set a heading, short list and action on one brand-colour half with a photograph filling the other. Use it at most twice.
Put a heading, two lines and one button in a narrow column beside three or four item cards. Repeat with the column on the same side for the next category.
Show each front in a portrait photograph with the street and one fact underneath.
Set the client’s name across the full wrap at the foot of the footer as the one oversized type moment.
Set the origin in one sentence at 40–56px with two or three little photographs in the line at text height.
Use the menu categories as the heading, the open one in ink and the others muted. Without script all categories show in order.
Show ingredients, materials or origins on square brand-ground tiles with one single-colour drawing and a name each.
Place four to six dated photographs on an offset grid around a short paragraph. Give each a white border and its year and keep the prints straight.
Show one identifiable record at its source and destination with the changed field legible in both.
Choose a supported environment and see its first working instruction, expected result and next action in the same panel.
Place a documented reading beside its object, unit, conditions and source.
Give each release its date, one line on what changed and aligned links to its real files.
Put related destinations under named headings, keep the most-used task within reach, and finish with a separate locale and policy row.
Set one dated change and its destination above the menu, leaving room for the notice to wrap and for a reader to dismiss it.
Show one complete operating record with its subject, event and time in a narrow band, with a pause control if the sample advances.
Group the direct install links by device, with an optional scan code beside the link for someone reading on another screen.
Place short accounts in reading-order columns and keep every speaker, context and source directly beneath their words.
Set a first-person account in one readable measure inside the wider page, ending at the writer’s name and role.
Group the named destinations by subject, align chapter references in a narrow track and link each title to its own heading.
Set a speaker’s account beside a separately sourced measure, with the population and period printed next to its number.
Give qualified claims numbered links to one reading column of conditions, with a return link for each place a condition was cited.
Let adjacent stages share a wide view of an ordered process, then unroll the same stages in reading order on a narrow screen.
Arrange editions as identifiable covers or spines with a chronological title list, each cover and title opening the same edition.
Place the available formats and their destinations under the title they serve, keeping each title’s choices together as the row wraps.
Place the enquiry fields beside a concrete view of what is being requested, keeping the submit action with its fields on a phone.
